results.name: outside_range_distance_slope
results.description: Among targets outside [min,max] of the examples, the OLS slope of yes on log(1 + distance to the nearest example); observed less negative than null means people's similarity gradient decays more slowly than the model's interval generalisation, more negative means a sharper fall-off.
results.code:
# name: outside_range_distance_slope
# description: Among targets outside [min,max] of the examples, the OLS slope of yes on log(1 + distance to the nearest example); observed less negative than null means people's similarity gradient decays more slowly than the model's interval generalisation, more negative means a sharper fall-off.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (t < lo) | (t > hi)
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = np.log1p(d[m]); y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()[m]
    if x.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0])

results.name: common_divisor_contrast
results.description: For multi-example sets whose GCD is >= 3, yes rate on targets divisible by that GCD minus non-divisible targets; observed below null means the model over-relies on multiples-of-k rules (people generalise along common factors less sharply), above null means it under-relies on them.
results.code:
# name: common_divisor_contrast
# description: For multi-example sets whose GCD is >= 3, yes rate on targets divisible by that GCD minus non-divisible targets; observed below null means the model over-relies on multiples-of-k rules (people generalise along common factors less sharply), above null means it under-relies on them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(e, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(np.int64).to_numpy()
    sel = (g >= 3) & (n >= 2)
    div = (t % np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = sel & div; b = sel & ~div
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; observed differing from null (~0) means responding drifts over the session (e.g. growing conservatism), which the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials where the target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means the model over-predicts certain "yes" for already-seen numbers (people are less deterministic / more lapse-prone there).

results.name: single_example_generalisation_rate
results.description: Yes rate for single-example sets on targets different from the example; observed above null means the model under-generalises from one example (too narrow), below null means it over-generalises.

results.name: within_cell_disagreement
results.description: Mean within-(set,target) Bernoulli variance p(1-p) of responses across repeated presentations of the same cell; observed above null means people disagree more than the model's (too extreme) predicted probabilities imply, below null means the model is too graded/uncertain.

results.name: set_size_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes rate (excluding targets that are examples) on the number of examples (1-4); observed less negative than null means people tighten generalisation with more examples less than the size principle predicts, more negative means they tighten more.
results.code:
# name: set_size_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes rate (excluding targets that are examples) on the number of examples (1-4); observed less negative than null means people tighten generalisation with more examples less than the size principle predicts, more negative means they tighten more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = ~(ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    x = n[m]; y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()[m]
    if len(x) < 3 or x.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0])

results.name: parity_match_contrast
results.description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate on parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching targets; observed above null means people use parity more than the model (model under-weights odd/even), below null means the model over-weights it.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_contrast
# description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate on parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching targets; observed above null means people use parity more than the model (model under-weights odd/even), below null means the model over-weights it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    pmin = np.nanmin(par, axis=1); pmax = np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    same = (pmin == pmax) & (n >= 2)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    match = (t % 2) == pmin
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = same & match; b = same & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
